title: Brazilian culture, regions and history
objectives: I can explain why the words of this unit are spelled, accented and pronounced as they are, using the rules of stress, nasal vowels and consonant groups.
I can read and discuss extended texts about Brazilian history, regions and traditions.
I can narrate historical events using the preterite, imperfect, pluperfect and the passive voice.
I can express cause, consequence and chronology in formal writing and read numbers, dates and percentages correctly.
I can separate the literal meaning of an expression from its natural English translation and from how it is used.

vocabulary.note: Built from the verb colonizar plus -ção, the ending that turns a verb into a feminine noun, like English -tion. The ç is the s sound before a, o or u. The z between vowels is a z sound, kept from colonizar. The ão is a nasal diphthong and is stressed on the last syllable by default, so no other accent is needed: ko-lo-ni-za-SÃO. Plural: colonizações.

example.pt: A colonização portuguesa começou no século dezesseis.
example.en: Portuguese colonization began in the sixteenth century.
example.literal: The colonization Portuguese began in-the century sixteen.

vocabulary.note: The prefix in- means not, so the word is not-dependence. It is stressed on dên. The circumflex on ê is the Brazilian convention for a stressed e before a nasal consonant (m or n) in the middle of a word. The ending ia counts as two vowels (in-de-pen-DÊN-ci-a), so the stress is on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, and the accent is always written. The c before i is s.

example.pt: A independência foi proclamada às margens do rio Ipiranga.
example.en: Independence was proclaimed on the banks of the Ipiranga River.
example.literal: The independence was proclaimed at-the margins of-the river Ipiranga.

vocabulary.note: From abolir plus -ção, like colonização: ç is s before o, and ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so no accent is needed. The abolition of slavery in Brazil came with the Lei Áurea of 1888, literally the Golden Law. Lei is the diphthong ei, and Áurea is stressed on Áu, third to last once the final ea counts as two vowels, so its accent is required.

example.pt: A abolição da escravidão foi um marco importante.
example.en: The abolition of slavery was an important milestone.
example.literal: The abolition of-the slavery was a mark important.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the third to last syllable (re-PÚ-bli-ca), which no ending predicts, so the acute accent is written on the stressed u. The letters bl stay together at the start of a syllable. Written with a capital R when it names the Brazilian Republic as a period of history, and with a small r for the form of government in general. The word comes from the Latin for public thing.

example.pt: A república foi proclamada pelos militares.
example.en: The republic was proclaimed by the military.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on pé. The ending io counts as two vowels, so the stress is third to last and the accent is required; it is acute because the e is open. The im at the start is a nasal vowel: m before p only nasalizes the i. Said im-PÉ-ryu, with the im nasal.

example.pt: O império durou pouco mais de sessenta anos.
example.en: The empire lasted a little over sixty years.
example.literal: The empire lasted little more of sixty years.

vocabulary.note: The m sits between two vowels, so it is an ordinary m. The g before r is the hard g of go, because the soft zh sound is only written with g before e or i. ção and ão work as in colonização. The prefix i- means into, as e- in emigração means out of.

example.pt: A imigração europeia transformou o Sul do país.
example.en: European immigration transformed the south of the country.

vocabulary.note: In most of Brazil d before an i sound is said like the j of judge: ji-ta-DU-ra. The t before a is an ordinary t. The stress is on du, the second to last syllable, which the final a predicts, so there is no accent. The military dictatorship in Brazil lasted from 1964 to 1985.

example.pt: A ditadura militar durou mais de vinte anos.
example.en: The military dictatorship lasted more than twenty years.

vocabulary.note: The prefix re- means again. In the middle, t before an i sound is said ch as in cheese: de-mo-kra-chi-za-SÃO. z between vowels is z, ç is s before a, and ão is stressed on the last syllable by default. The word at the start has the strong r, said like a breathy English h.

vocabulary.en: quilombo, a settlement of escaped enslaved people
vocabulary.note: qu before i writes the k sound and the u is silent: ki-LÕ-bu. The m in lom stands before b, so it only nasalizes the vowel. Stress on lom, the second to last syllable, as a final o predicts. The most famous quilombo was Palmares, led by Zumbi.

example.pt: O Quilombo dos Palmares resistiu por quase um século.
example.en: The Quilombo dos Palmares resisted for almost a century.

vocabulary.note: g before i is the zh sound, like the s of measure. The i and ão are two separate syllables, so the word has three: he-zhi-ÃO. The first r is the strong r. The plural is regiões, a nasal ending stressed on the last syllable. The five regions are Norte, Nordeste, Centro-Oeste, Sudeste and Sul.

example.en: Brazil is divided into five regions.
example.literal: The Brazil itself divides in five regions.

vocabulary.note: The dry, thinly populated interior of the Northeast. ão is the nasal diphthong, stressed on the last syllable by default, so no accent. The r before t ends its syllable, and how it sounds varies by region. Plural: sertões.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on zô. The ô is closed, and the circumflex is the convention for a stressed o before a nasal consonant (m or n) in the middle of a word. vocabulary.note: Written with a capital letter when it means the festival. A final l is said like w, and a word ending in l is stressed on the last syllable by default, so there is no accent: kah-na-VAW. The r before n ends its syllable and varies by region.

vocabulary.note: A círio is a large wax candle carried in processions. The word is stressed on the first syllable, third to last because io counts as two vowels, so the accent is written. Nazaré is stressed on the last syllable although it ends in e, which breaks the default, so the open é takes an accent; z between vowels is z. vocabulary.en: boi-bumbá, the folk dance of the ox
vocabulary.note: A compound word joined by a hyphen. Boi is ox, and oi is a diphthong said like English boy. Bumbá is a name of the tradition, not an ordinary word. It is stressed on the last syllable, which a final a does not predict, so the acute is written; um is nasal and the m stands before b. In Parintins, in the state of Amazonas, two teams, Garantido and Caprichoso, compete.

example.en: The boi-bumbá of Parintins gathers thousands of people.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: accents and stress in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
This unit is full of historical and cultural names, and many of them carry accents. The stress lesson gives one method that explains every one of them, and it never changes: divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable by ear, read the default stress from the ending, and compare. By default a word ending in a, e or o (with or without s), or in am, em or ens, is stressed on the second to last syllable. A word ending in anything else (i, u, is, us, l, r, z, im, um, ns, a nasal ã or ão, or a diphthong such as ei or ou) is stressed on the last syllable. If the stress agrees with the default, no accent is written. If it disagrees, the stressed vowel carries an accent. An accent is therefore never decoration: it says that the word breaks the default of its ending.

Three kinds of word carry accents here. The first are words stressed on the third to last syllable, called proparoxytones. No ending predicts that position, so the accent is always written: república, século, fábricas, típico, elétricos, parágrafo, último. This includes words that end in a glide plus a vowel (ia, io, ea), because the spelling rule counts the i as a syllable of its own: in-de-pen-DÊN-ci-a, a-ma-ZÔ-ni-a, CÍ-ri-o, im-PÉ-ri-o, bra-ZÍ-li-a. Compare Bahia, economia and monarquia, where the stressed syllable is the i itself (ba-HI-a, e-co-no-MI-a, mo-nar-QUI-a). That is the second to last syllable, which the final a already predicts, so no accent is needed.

The second kind are words stressed on the last syllable although they end in a, e, o or em, which predict stress earlier: Nazaré, acarajé, bumbá, forró, Belém, está, Pará. The accent is written on the stressed vowel. Stressed one-syllable words that end in a, e or o, with or without s, are always marked (já, há, dá, vá, é, só, mês); the small unstressed words a, o, e, de and que are not. The mark also keeps há (there is, or ago) apart from the small word a, and é (is) apart from e (and). The verb form têm has a circumflex to show the plural: ele tem, eles têm. The stressed syllable is the same; only the mark tells singular from plural.

The third kind are words that look as if they need an accent but do not. A word ending in the nasal ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, and the tilde already marks both the nasal sound and that stress, so colonização, abolição, sertão, região, milhão and violão need nothing more. The same holds for plurals in -ões, such as regiões and milhões. Verb forms that end in the diphthong ou, eu or iu, or in ei (durou, nasceu, resistiu, provei), are stressed on the last syllable, which is the default for a final glide, so they carry no accent either. The open diphthongs éi, éu and ói are the exception, because the acute shows the open vowel (céu, herói). A stressed i or u that follows another vowel in a separate syllable (a hiatus) is marked when it stands alone in its syllable or is followed only by s: reúne is re-Ú-ne, país is pa-ÍS. Without the accent, eu would be read as one beat, a diphthong.

Which accent? The acute marks a stressed vowel. On e and o it also shows that the vowel is open (e as in bed, o as in law), and on a it marks the open a of father; i and u have only one quality, so í and ú mark only stress or a hiatus. The circumflex marks a stressed closed e or o (ê as in say, ô as in go). Before m or n the vowel is nasal, and the convention is the circumflex in the middle of a word (independência, Amazônia) and the acute at the end of a word before m (Belém, também). Everywhere else the quality of e and o is learned with the word, and the mark records it.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: consonants, nasal vowels and letter groups in the new words
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese spelling is regular because every sound has a small set of spellings, and the choice between them follows from the letters next to it. This note applies the rules of the sound lesson to the new words, so that nothing in this unit is left unexplained. The table groups the words by rule.

Start with c and g, which each have two sounds chosen by the vowel that follows. Before a, o or u, c is k and g is the g of go. Before e or i, c is s and g is zh, the s of measure. Portuguese keeps the system symmetrical by giving each sound a second spelling. To get k or g before e or i, add a silent u: qu and gu (moqueca, quilombo, esqueça, Pixinguinha). To get s before a, o or u, use the cedilla: ç (dança, colonização, esqueça). To get zh before any vowel, use j, which always has that sound (feijoada, junina, laranja, hoje). The hard g also stays in front of r, because only e and i soften it (imigração, Grande). The u of qu and gu is said before a (quadrilha, quando, desigualdades), and in a few words before e or i, which you learn with the word.

Next the s family. A single s between vowels is z (religiosa, Isabel), so the double ss exists to write the s sound between vowels (procissão, impressionante, dezesseis, sessenta), and sc is simply s (nasceu). At the end of a syllable, before a consonant, s is s or sh depending on the region (festa, escravidão). The letter z is z between vowels (dezenove), and a final z is said like a final s (arroz). The letter x has several values: sh (abacaxi, Pixinguinha), z in the ex- that begins a word before a vowel (exato), and s before a consonant (texto). The x of trouxe is an exception, said s, which you learn with the word. The digraphs ch, lh and nh are one sound each and are never split when dividing a word: ch is sh (choro, chimarrão, churrasco, chegaram), lh is ly (milhão, quadrilha, trabalharam), nh is ny (cavaquinho).

The letter r has two sounds. At the start of a word, and when doubled between vowels, it is the strong r, said like a breathy English h: república, região, redemocratização, forró, churrasco. A single r between vowels or inside a consonant group is a quick tap of the tongue, close to the tt of American butter: ditadura, período, imigração, Brasil. At the end of a syllable, as in sertão, Carnaval or Nordeste, how r sounds varies by region, and you adapt to the speakers around you.

Nasal vowels come from the letters m and n. A vowel followed by m or n that ends the syllable is nasal, and the m or n is not said as a consonant: samba, quilombo, império, Campina, Grande, independência, importante, Parintins, margens. The letter is m before b and p and n before every other consonant. When m or n stands between two vowels it starts the next syllable and is an ordinary consonant (imigração, Amazônia, baianas). The tilde makes ã and õ nasal, and the common endings are ão and ões.

Three sound shifts are typical of Brazilian speech. First, l at the end of a syllable is said like w (Brasil, Carnaval, Salvador, alguma). Second, in most of the country d and t before an i sound are said like the j of judge and the ch of cheese: ditadura (ji), típico (chi). The i sound includes a final unstressed e, which is said i, so grande is GRÃN-ji, importante ends in chi, tarde in ji and Nordeste in chi. A final unstressed o is said u (choro, SHO-ru). Third, h is never said on its own (hoje, havia, habitantes, Bahia); it only works inside ch, lh and nh.

Finally, two vowels written together may be one beat or two. A strong vowel (a, e, o) next to a weak i or u glides into one beat, a diphthong: ei in feijoada and Lei, oi in boi, ou in durou. Two strong vowels, a stressed weak vowel, or a weak vowel in front of the ending ão form a hiatus and take separate beats: região is re-gi-ão, feijoada is fei-jo-a-da, país is pa-ís. A hyphen joins the parts of a compound (boi-bumbá, Centro-Oeste, afro-brasileira) and joins a pronoun to its verb (tornou-se, fundou-se, destaca-se). The pronoun is unstressed and the stress does not move, so tornou-se is tor-NOU-si.

grammar.title: Reading strategies for extended texts
grammar.explanation:
A text is not a pile of sentences. It is built in layers. A paragraph has one topic, usually stated in its first sentence, which is called the topic sentence (frase-tópico in Portuguese). The sentences inside the paragraph are linked by small words called connectors, which say how one idea relates to the next: contrast, cause, consequence, addition, order in time. Reading well means using that structure instead of translating word by word. Historical and cultural texts suit the method because they are dense with names, dates and numbers, and the connectors carry the logic that holds those facts together.

Read in three passes. First skim, which means reading fast for the general idea: the title, the first and last paragraphs, and the first sentence of each paragraph. Then scan, which means hunting with the eyes for one kind of item, such as names, dates, numbers or places. Only then read closely and follow the connectors. The connectors of contrast (porém, contudo, no entanto), cause (porque, devido a), consequence (portanto, por isso), addition (além disso) and order (em seguida, posteriormente) come from the lessons on connectors and on formal writing, and the next notes of this unit show how to build sentences with them. What is new here is using them as signposts. When you meet porém, the next clause will go against the previous one, so you can predict the meaning before you read it.

Portuguese also has expressions that tell you whose position a sentence reports, which matters in history because facts and interpretations are mixed. Segundo o autor and de acordo com os historiadores name the source. Segundo is not used for your own view (never segundo mim); for that say na minha opinião or para mim. Verbs such as defender que, sugerir que and afirmar que report what a text claims, and tratar de means to deal with. Defender also means to defend or protect, as in English, but followed by que it means to argue that: the author is making an argument.

After reading, check your comprehension by paraphrasing, which means saying each paragraph in one sentence of your own. If you cannot, reread. In comprehension questions, a wrong answer is often true but answers a different question, or takes a detail from another paragraph. Go back to the passage and find the sentence that answers the question asked, instead of answering from memory.

grammar.title: Historical narration: preterite, imperfect, pluperfect, passive and historical present
grammar.explanation:
A story about the past has two layers. The first is the line of events, the things that happened one after another. The second is the circumstances: what the situation was, what was going on, what people used to do. Portuguese gives each layer its own tense, and history writing switches between them all the time. English has one simple past (declared, depended) and adds helpers to show the second layer (was depending, used to depend). Portuguese shows it in the verb ending.

The preterite (pretérito perfeito) narrates a completed event, seen as a point or as a whole with a limit: Dom Pedro Primeiro declarou a independência. The imperfect (pretérito imperfeito) describes a background state, a habit or a repeated action with no stated limit: A economia dependia do trabalho escravo. Muitos imigrantes chegavam ao porto de Santos. One verb can take either tense, depending on how the writer sees the situation. O Brasil era colônia describes the state as scenery. O Brasil foi colônia por mais de trezentos anos sums it up as a finished period with a limit. A good test is to ask whether the action is closed and counted, which calls for the preterite, or is scenery or routine, which calls for the imperfect.

The pluperfect (mais-que-perfeito) marks an event that was already finished before another past moment, as English had does: Quando a república foi proclamada, o imperador já havia perdido o apoio político. It is built from the imperfect of ter or haver plus a participle, the verb form that ends in -ado or -ido (perdido, começado) and is also used in the passive. Haver is the formal choice in writing and ter the everyday one; the meaning is the same. A second, one-word form exists in formal and literary prose. Fora is the pluperfect of ser and ir, made by taking the third person plural of the preterite (foram) and dropping the m: Até então, o Brasil fora colônia de Portugal, meaning had been. You need to recognize it when reading more than to use it.

The passive voice makes the receiver of the action the subject. Three terms: the subject is what the verb is about, the agent is the one who performs the action, and in the passive the agent is introduced by por or left out. The recipe, from the passive lesson, is ser in the tense of the active verb plus the participle, which agrees with the new subject in gender and number like an adjective: A república foi proclamada, A Lei Áurea foi assinada pela princesa Isabel, Os escravizados foram libertados. The agent follows por, which fuses with the article (por + a = pela, por + os = pelos). History favors the passive because the writer often does not know or care who acted, and because the focus is the event. The second passive uses se, and the verb agrees with the receiver: Fundou-se a cidade de São Paulo, Fundaram-se duas vilas. Here se does not mean himself; it only marks that no agent is named. Because formal writing avoids opening a sentence with a pronoun, se follows the verb and is joined to it by a hyphen, as in the pronoun placement lesson. The same placement appears with tornar-se, to become: O país tornou-se uma monarquia.

Finally, the historical present. The present tense can tell past events when the writer wants them to feel immediate: Em mil oitocentos e vinte e dois, Dom Pedro declara a independência. It is common in headlines, museum captions and timelines, and it usually comes with a date that anchors it in the past. English does the same in headlines (Napoleon invades Russia). Keep one choice inside a passage: do not slide between the historical present and the preterite without a reason.

grammar.title: Cause, consequence and chronology
grammar.explanation:
Events in history connect in two ways: by time (when, for how long, before or after) and by logic (what caused what). Portuguese has a word for each relation, and the most useful thing to know is the grammatical kind of the word, because the kind decides what may follow it. Three terms are needed. A preposition is a short word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence (de, em, por). A clause is a group of words with its own conjugated verb, and a conjunction links one clause to another. A noun phrase is a noun with its article and adjectives, for example a crise do café.

Cause before a noun phrase. Devido a, em virtude de, em decorrência de, por causa de and graças a are prepositions, so they take a noun phrase and never a conjugated verb: Devido à crise do café, muitas fazendas faliram. Devido a ends in the preposition a, so with a feminine noun it fuses with the article a and takes the grave accent (devido à crise), and with a masculine noun it becomes ao (devido ao aumento). The others fuse with de in the usual way (em virtude da crise, por causa do preço). They differ in tone: devido a, em virtude de and em decorrência de belong to writing, por causa de is neutral, and graças a names a good cause, its literal sense being thanks to.

Cause before a clause. Porque, visto que, uma vez que, já que and como at the start of a sentence are conjunctions, so they take a clause with its own verb: Como a seca durou anos, muitas famílias migraram. Portuguese keeps the two groups apart, so devido a is never followed directly by a conjugated verb.

Consequence. Portanto, por isso, assim and então open a new clause and are followed by the verb: A seca durou anos; por isso, muitas famílias migraram. Verbs can also carry the relation from inside the sentence. Provocar, causar and acarretar take the cause as the subject and the effect as the direct object: A seca provocou a migração. Resultar em and levar a put a preposition before the effect: A seca levou à migração, with a + a fusing to à. And o que, the relative pronoun of the relatives lesson, can sum up a whole clause: A seca provocou a migração de milhares de famílias, o que levou ao crescimento das cidades. English does this with which. Here o que refers to the whole idea before it, not to one noun. Do not treat sequence as causation: depois de only says that something came later, while por causa de says why.

Time. Em names a point: em mil oitocentos e vinte e dois, no século dezenove (em + o). Durante gives a period seen as a whole, and ao longo de gives a period in which something develops gradually. Desde names a starting point that continues up to now or up to another reference point. De ... até and entre ... e give both limits. A partir de names a starting point after which something changes: A partir de mil novecentos e sessenta, a capital passou a ser Brasília. The verb phrases passar a (to come to be) and voltar a (to go back to being) say that a state changed, and both take an infinitive. Antes de and depois de take a noun or an infinitive, and após is a formal synonym of depois de. The order of events in a paragraph is shown by primeiro, em seguida, posteriormente, mais tarde, logo depois and finalmente, and a reference point in the past by até então (up to that moment) and desde então (from that moment on).

One last point is há, from haver. With a time expression it does two jobs that English keeps apart. Há dois dias means two days ago. With a verb in the present, it means for: O sertão sofre com a seca há séculos, where English needs the present perfect (has suffered). In the past, the imperfect havia gives had been for: Os povos indígenas já viviam aqui havia milênios.

grammar.title: Numbers, dates and percentages in formal texts
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese texts write numbers in digits and read them as chains of words, and the chain follows fixed rules. A year is read as one full number; there is no shortening like the English nineteen eighty-eight. The number 1888 is mil oitocentos e oitenta e oito, and 2024 is dois mil e vinte e quatro. The word e joins the last elements of a chain. It comes between hundreds, tens and units (oitocentos e oitenta e oito), and it comes after mil only when what follows is a round hundred or a number below one hundred: mil e quinhentos (1500), mil e cem, dois mil e vinte e quatro. When the rest has several parts, there is no e after mil: mil quinhentos e cinquenta e quatro (1554), mil oitocentos e vinte e dois (1822), mil novecentos e sessenta (1960).

A date is written day, month, year, joined by de, with the month in lower case: 7 de setembro de 1822 is read sete de setembro de mil oitocentos e vinte e dois. A cardinal number counts (um, dois, três) and an ordinal number ranks (primeiro, segundo, terceiro). Dates use cardinals (sete, quinze) except for the first day of the month, which is an ordinal: 1º de maio is primeiro de maio. The small raised o in 1º marks the masculine ordinal, and ª marks the feminine. The first of the month is the only day named as the first by convention.

Roman numerals are used for centuries and rulers. The symbols are I (1), V (5), X (10), L (50) and C (100). A smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted, so IX is 9 and XIX is 19. A century is read with a cardinal from eleven on: século XIX is século dezenove and século XX is século vinte. For centuries up to ten the formal reading is an ordinal (século quinto), though speakers often use the cardinal here too. Rulers are read as ordinals up to ten: Dom Pedro I is Dom Pedro Primeiro and Dom Pedro II is Dom Pedro Segundo. The spellings dezesseis, dezessete, dezoito and dezenove need care: they are dez- plus the unit, and the s of dezesseis and dezessete is doubled to keep the s sound between vowels.

Percentages use por cento, literally by hundred: 42% is quarenta e dois por cento. Parts of a whole are metade (half), um terço, dois terços, um quarto and três quartos, and mais da metade means more than half. Portuguese writes decimals with a comma and separates thousands with a period: 3,5 milhões is três vírgula cinco milhões, and 100.000 is cem mil. Milhão, bilhão and trilhão are nouns, so they need de before the thing counted (um milhão de habitantes, dois bilhões de reais). Mil and cem are not nouns and take no de (cem mil habitantes). In writing, these nouns stay singular up to 1,99 (1,2 bilhão) and are plural from two (2,5 bilhões). Bilhão is a thousand million, like the English billion, and trilhão is the English trillion. A decade names only its tens: nos anos sessenta or na década de sessenta is the 1960s.

The verb that follows a percentage agrees with what comes next. If a noun follows, the verb takes the number of that noun: Quarenta por cento da população vive no Sudeste (população is singular), Quarenta por cento dos brasileiros vivem no Sudeste (brasileiros is plural). If the percentage stands alone, the verb agrees with the number: Um por cento concordou, Dois por cento concordaram. In formal prose, spell out numbers up to about ten and round numbers such as cem, mil and um milhão, and use digits for precise data: 14,7% da população.

grammar.title: Small words and expressions in the dialogues: literal meaning and use
grammar.explanation:
Every language has expressions whose literal meaning and real use drift apart, and the dialogues of this unit contain several. The habit this course asks of you is to read each one twice. First read it literally, word for word in Portuguese order, to see what the words actually say. Then read it as a native speaker uses it. The two readings answer different questions, and neither replaces the other. The table gives both for the expressions in the dialogues, and the dialogue lines carry the literal glosses.

Some of the drift is grammar. Portuguese says Depende do que você procura (depends of-the what you look-for) because depender takes the preposition de, and de fuses with o que to give do que. It says a gente costuma comer where English says we usually eat, with gente, people, as a singular subject. It uses the pattern vou escolher (I-go to-choose) for the near future and vamos ouvir (we-go to-hear) for a suggestion, both built on the verb ir. It uses dá para ver (gives to see) for being possible, with dar para plus an infinitive. It uses the verb levar, to take, for what a recipe contains: A moqueca leva leite de coco. It uses virar, to turn, for becoming: A feijoada virou um prato nacional. And it leaves out a noun when it is clear: a capixaba is the moqueca from Espírito Santo, and capixaba, the adjective for that state, is used as a noun here.

Some of the drift is history. Nossa, an exclamation of surprise, began as Nossa Senhora, Our Lady. Dona in dona Neide comes from the Latin for lady and is a respectful title for a woman before her first name. Obrigada, thanks, is the feminine form of obliged: a woman says obrigada and a man says obrigado, because the adjective agrees with the speaker. These are now ordinary words whose literal meaning most speakers no longer notice. Learn the literal sense once, then use the expression as speakers do.

One more case shows the difference between tenses in the two languages. Eu nunca fui is literally I never went, and it means I have never been. Portuguese uses the simple past where English uses the present perfect, and Está tocando desde cedo uses the present progressive with desde where English says has been playing since early.

culture.title: Um país de muitos Brasis
culture.text:
Brazil is often described as a country of many Brazils. Indigenous peoples lived on the land for thousands of years before the arrival of the Portuguese in 1500, and many words in everyday Portuguese come from Tupi: abacaxi, mandioca, jabuticaba, Ipanema. Their spelling follows the same rules as any other word. In abacaxi the x is said sh and the stress is on the last syllable, as the final i predicts (a-ba-ka-SHI). In jabuticaba the j is zh, and in mandioca the d before i is said j (man-ji-O-ka). Millions of Africans were brought to Brazil as enslaved people over more than three centuries, and their influence shaped samba, capoeira, candomblé, acarajé and a large part of the language. Quilombos such as Palmares, led by Zumbi, were communities of resistance. Since 2024, the twentieth of November, the Dia da Consciência Negra, has been a national holiday.

After the abolition of slavery in 1888, millions of Europeans, and later Japanese, Lebanese and others, came as immigrants. Italians settled in São Paulo and the South, Germans in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul, and the Japanese community of Liberdade, in São Paulo, is one of the largest outside Japan. The result is a mixture visible in food, music, religion and festivals, from the Carnival of Rio to the Círio de Nazaré in Belém, the June festivals of the Northeast and the boi-bumbá of Parintins.

Brazil is also divided into five official regions, Norte, Nordeste, Centro-Oeste, Sudeste and Sul, each with its own character, climate and accent. The country has 26 states and a Federal District, where Brasília, inaugurated in 1960, replaced Rio de Janeiro as the capital. Understanding this diversity is the best way to understand why a single word such as moqueca or forró can mean something slightly different from one state to another.

exercises.prompt: Why does independência carry an accent?
